candidate_workflows: Give strong makers a clearly owned component, a high-level objective, and autonomy over details; combine collaboration with individual ownership instead of routing every decision through management.
Evaluate future founders and technical teammates by the ambitious projects they chose and completed, not just grades or credentials, and use playful side projects as a source of startup ideas.
At a project's start, lower the standard enough to begin; once the work exists, raise the standard through iteration rather than letting fear of failure prevent the first attempt.
title: A Project of One's Own

candidate_workflows: Separate necessary work from credential exercises and busywork, then aim daily effort toward the hardest important part of the problem rather than clearing easy peripheral tasks.
Find a sustainable work limit by monitoring output quality, not hours performed; adjust as task difficulty and capacity change, and treat both laziness and overwork as calibration errors.
Audit whether interest, talent, and results still justify the current field or project; allow enough time to gain traction, but switch when sustained effort does not produce sufficiently good work.
Check whether money, status, or others' expectations are distorting what you believe is interesting, and make motivation explicit before committing to ambitious work.
title: How to Work Hard

candidate_workflows: To expand a maker's technical repertoire, choose a language considered weird whose median user is strong, isolate how it differs from the common intersection of popular languages, ask what it expresses that would be impractical elsewhere, and use the comparison to discover new ways to think about and build software.
title: Weird Languages

candidate_workflows: Evaluate founders and idea-generating teammates by the important new ideas and solved problems they produce, not by conversational quickness or a general impression of intelligence.

Cultivate new-idea output as a system: combine deep interest, independent judgment, owned projects, hard work, restorative conditions, strong colleagues, and written exploration instead of treating originality as a fixed trait.
Write about a domain to expose tacit knowledge and discover ideas that were not fully formed before drafting; expect substantial reworking when a better question appears.
title: Beyond Smart

candidate_workflows: Evaluate product or creative quality by its intended effect on a shared human audience, while accepting a partial rather than total ordering when informed observers disagree.
Calibrate taste through repeated making and comparison with strong work, and discount fame, prestige, social expectation, and other extraneous influences during review.
Use knowledgeable observers and controlled comparisons rather than a raw popularity vote when judging whether a design performs its purpose.
title: Is There Such a Thing as Good Taste?

candidate_workflows: Turn a complex strategy, product claim, or decision into prose, reread it as a neutral stranger with no access to unstated context, and repeatedly rewrite, qualify, add, or cut until it is correct and complete.
Use writing to surface unconscious domain knowledge and discover missing ideas; discard plans that remain broken when made explicit instead of preserving the feeling that they are complete.
For important ill-defined questions, prefer a written treatment over conversation alone because writing forces one exact sequence that can be inspected and revised.
title: Putting Ideas into Words

exclusion_reason: A political and social argument about ideological orthodoxy, punishment, and freedom of expression; it supplies no startup-specific decision, product practice, user method, team process, or operating workflow.
title: Heresy

candidate_workflows: Ask founders to explain what they learned from users; use the specificity of the answer to test whether they observe users closely, understand their needs, and have evidence of urgency.
Diagnose a reported fundraising or acquisition problem by checking the underlying company and product, then rank all known problems by survival impact and put the lethal one first.

Choose the most important problem, then use the shortest experiment interval that can produce trustworthy evidence: a week or less is useful when results arrive that fast, investor negotiations may fit days, and hardware may require months; act, measure, and correct course at that cadence so short-term decisions remain decisive while long-term direction stays provisional.
When individualized advising stops scaling, shard companies into stable groups with dedicated advisers who know their context instead of making every adviser track every company.
Deliberately build a founder peer cluster that supplies colleagues, practical help, candid comparison, and morale in addition to expert advice.
title: What I've Learned from Users

exclusion_reason: A philosophical proposal to seek truths that any intelligent species might share; it offers no concrete startup, maker, product, user, team, work, or communication procedure.
title: Alien Truth

exclusion_reason: A metaphysical reflection on free will and higher-order desires; it contains no founder decision method, team practice, product or user process, operating guidance, or maker workflow.
title: What You (Want to)* Want

candidate_workflows: When a founder or maker faces a complicated ill-defined problem, write through it to expose new structure and ideas; use conversation as input, not as a substitute for the written pass.
Maintain a diet of strong writing and read for meaning as well as information, because reading quality constrains the writing ability used to solve and communicate difficult problems.
title: The Need to Read

candidate_workflows: Build enough domain depth to reach a knowledge frontier, keep track of what seems strange, missing, or broken, and investigate the gaps that remain obvious after expertise rather than brainstorming startup ideas in the abstract.
title: How to Get New Ideas

candidate_workflows: Choose a field by the intersection of aptitude and deep interest, test the choice through owned projects, and switch when the work does not become more interesting as knowledge grows.
Reach a frontier, record anomalies and neglected questions, and pursue an outlier only when expertise lets you explain precisely what others overlook.
Protect contiguous blocks for hard work, monitor quality to find the sustainable daily limit, and cross the activation barrier with a deliberately tiny first action.

Identify work whose returns compound through durable learning, product, or audience loops; do a small amount consistently rather than alternating bursts with zero, expect the early curve to feel flat, and consider disproportionate initial effort to get the loop started.
Start with the simplest version that could work, put it in front of real users quickly, and evolve it through successive versions without loading every new idea into one release.
Audit work for affectation, inconsistency, and sunk-cost attachment; use the reversal question to decide whether to redo or cut something that no longer fits.

Treat setbacks as local backtracking rather than a verdict on the goal, protect morale with visible progress and a small dedicated audience, and choose a few colleagues who provide surprising insight and energy.
title: How to Do Great Work

candidate_workflows: Track startup growth rate rather than early absolute size, and use changes in the rate as a compass for what to improve next.
Seek loops where each cycle builds infrastructure, audience, brand, or learning that improves the next; count a failed attempt as progress only when it compounds capability.

Investigate mediocre but popular products as replacement opportunities, then check for hidden barriers such as monopoly, regulation, or broken buying procedures before treating popularity as proof of demand for an alternative.
Apply disproportionate personal attention to a tiny initial customer set to start word of mouth when the product has a plausible compounding distribution loop.
Choose high-variance work only when the upside, skill, and personal circumstances justify exposure, and take multiple affordable shots instead of requiring one bet to succeed.
title: Superlinear Returns

candidate_workflows: Begin an important memo with a puzzling question where you have an insight or unexplained gap, commit an initial answer to words, and reread strictly for correctness and completeness until hidden assumptions surface.
Treat exploration as a branching tree: follow the branch with the strongest combination of novelty and generality, then backtrack and cut quickly when it fails, regardless of sunk effort.

Generate stronger questions by combining broad, diverse inputs with depth from doing hard work in a domain, and spend time with people who reliably cause new ideas rather than maximizing the number of contacts.
Cast a wide net for questions and be exacting with answers; use repeated rewriting to turn inspiration into a defensible piece of founder or product communication.
title: The Best Essay

candidate_workflows: Develop technical ability through self-directed projects that produce something, choosing subjects by genuine interest and practicing across multiple projects instead of relying on coursework alone.

For young founders, whose own needs are more predictive and whose knowledge of other users is limited, use technical expertise to notice missing or broken things, build a fix for themselves and friends, and test whether those friends would be genuinely upset to lose it; treat this as the best initial idea source for this stage, not the only source.
Let useful projects become companies after demand appears rather than starting with an abstract company idea or premature monetization plan.
Choose cofounders by working on projects together first; require demonstrated skill and evidence that the group works well under real task pressure.

For a pre-college student who may found later, build technical skill through projects while doing well enough in school to preserve access to a selective university; use it as a dense network of potential cofounders, early employees, and project-generated ideas, not as a prestige or teaching credential, and remember it is a common source rather than the only route.
Before forming the company, verify the three prerequisites separately: technical capability, a concrete thing to build, and one or two proven cofounders.
title: How to Start Google

candidate_workflows: Reject an initial idea whose launch depends on too many unavailable partners without discarding a high-energy team; pivot the founders to a nearby need supported by direct behavior or traffic evidence.
Look for founder-product fit in traits that improve the product's mechanism and culture, such as curiosity for a discovery product or skepticism toward editorial control.
Constrain version one to the smallest implementation that can launch within weeks, then seed the first content and users manually rather than waiting for an organic cold start.
When traffic is initially noisy, look for a small core returning regularly; treat repeated use as the earliest evidence that the product has durable utility.
title: The Reddits

candidate_workflows: Test determination by how someone reacts to disagreement: persistent founders actively inspect possible holes, while obstinate ones defend doctrine or stop listening.
Hold the high-level goal more firmly than any implementation detail; revise low-level tactics as evidence changes their expected value instead of confusing the first plan with the mission.
Build persistence as a system of energy, imagination, resilience, judgment, and focus: keep generating paths, protect morale from setbacks, and backtrack only as far as the evidence requires.
Set a goal specific enough to direct the next action but broad enough to admit adjacent discoveries; when inexperienced, start slightly narrow and expand once movement creates information.
title: The Right Kind of Stubborn
